Objectives: Technologies supporting the continuous, real-time measurement of blood oxygen saturation and plasma glucose levels have improved our ability to monitor performance status. Our ability to monitor other molecular markers of performance, however, including the hormones known to indicate overtraining and general health, has lagged. That is, although a number of other molecular markers of performance status have been identified, we have struggled to develop viable technologies supporting their real-time monitoring in the body. Here we review biosensor approaches that may support such measurements, as well as the molecules potentially of greatest interest to monitor. Design: Narrative literature review. Method: Literature review. Results: Significant effort has been made to harness the specificity, affinity, and generalizability of biomolecular recognition in a platform technology supporting continuous in vivo molecular measurements. Most biosensor approaches, however, are either not generalizable to most targets, or fail when challenged in the complex environments found in vivo. Electrochemical aptamer-based sensors, in contrast, are the first technology to simultaneously achieve both of these critical attributes. In an effort to illustrate the potential of this platform technology, we both critically review the literature describing it and briefly survey some of the molecular performance markers we believe will prove advantageous to monitor using it. Conclusions: Electrochemical aptamer-based sensors may be the first truly generalizable technology for monitoring specific molecules in situ in the body and how adaptation of the platform to subcutaneous microneedles will enable the real-time monitoring of performance markers via a wearable, minimally invasive device Wearable electronic devices Electrochemistry Technology Aptamers Pharmacokinetics Health monitoring 1. Introduction Although few in number, the technologies supporting real-time molecular measurements in the body have significantly impacted our ability to monitor human performance status. The pulse oximeter, for example, which reports changes in blood oxygen levels in real-time, has rapidly expanded from a specialty surgical technology to a ubiquitous clinical and performance-monitoring tool. 1 By providing real-time information on blood sugar levels, wearable continuous glucose monitors have similarly revolutionized the treatment of diabetes, and are making rapid inroads into performance monitoring. 2 , 3 Beyond oxygen and glucose, however, our ability to monitor specific molecules in the body in real time remains limited. For example, while in January 2022, medical device provider Abbott Laboratories announced their wearable biosensor Lingo product line to continuously monitor ketones, lactate, alcohol, and glucose, these devices are not yet commercially available. 4 Beyond this, until recently, only a handful of other molecules have been measured in real-time in vivo, even just as laboratory demonstrations (e.g., glutamate, acetylcholine). 5 – 7 The glucose monitor and the pulse oximeter are biosensors, a class of technologies that has long been promised to be general, but that has yet to realize this vision in in vivo applications. The problem is, like all previous approaches to in vivo molecular monitoring, the glucose monitor and the pulse oximeter rely critically on the chemical reactivity of their targets. Specifically, glucose sensors use glucose oxidase to convert its target into an easily measurable product (hydrogen peroxide), and the pulse oximeter monitors the color change that occurs when oxygen binds to hemoglobin. 1 , 8 And, although we can now generate proteins and nucleic acids that will recognize almost any water-soluble target, 9 we cannot generate peroxide-producing enzymes or color-changing receptors at will, thus greatly limiting the extent to which sensing approaches analogous to the glucose meter or the pulse oximeter can be expanded to new targets. In short, achieving the goal of a generalizable ability to monitor specific molecules in the body will require the development of technologies that are independent of the chemical reactivity of their targets. For many years, the primary focus of efforts to build biosensor “platforms” that are independent of the reactivity of their targets has been “adsorption-based” biosensors that rely on target detection via changes in mass, charge, steric bulk or optical properties associated with the adsorption of the target to a biomolecular receptor attached to a surface. Examples of this include sensors based on surface plasmon resonance, field effect transistors, quartz crystal microbalances, and microcantilevers. 10 , 11 Unfortunately, however, when challenged in bodily fluids these approaches are overwhelmed by the non-specific adsorption of proteins, which produces signals that are indistinguishable from those produced by authentic target binding. 12 , 13 In contrast to most biosensor architectures, the chemoperception systems found in nature are both selective enough to work in vivo and independent of the chemical reactivity of their targets. 14 To achieve both of these attributes simultaneously, evolution designed the relevant receptors such that they undergo a large-scale conformational change upon target binding. 15 This, in turn, generates an output that is not mimicked by non-specific adsorption. Inspired by this naturally occurring phenomenon, a new class of artificial biosensors, termed electrochemical, aptamer-based (EAB) sensors, has recently achieved the breakthrough milestone of monitoring molecules in vivo without relying on their reactivity ( Fig. 1 ). 16 – 22 In this review, we first describe EAB sensors before then surveying in vivo EAB sensor literature. Finally, we close by discussing the adaptation of EAB sensors to performance monitoring.

extracted_data.document_summary: This narrative literature review investigates biosensor approaches for continuous, real-time in vivo monitoring of molecular markers relevant to performance and health status. It highlights the limitations of current technologies and proposes electrochemical aptamer-based (EAB) sensors as a generalizable, minimally invasive solution. The review details the development, validation, and attributes (generalizability, selectivity, reversibility, stability) of EAB sensors for detecting diverse targets (drugs, metabolites, hormones, proteins) in complex biological fluids and tissues. It also addresses the technological hurdles for subcutaneous placement, the correlation between interstitial fluid and systemic concentrations, and their potential for monitoring stress indicators (e.g., cortisol) and HPA/HPG axis hormones to assess overtraining syndromes.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Electrochemical Aptamer-Based (EAB) Sensor Technology for Real-time In Vivo Molecular Monitoring
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This narrative literature review discusses the development and application of Electrochemical Aptamer-Based (EAB) sensors for continuous, real-time in vivo molecular monitoring, without an applied 'dose' in the traditional sense as it is a review of technology. EAB sensors, including 75-µm-diameter, 3-mm-long versions, have been tested in live rats for plasma monitoring (jugular vein) for up to 12 hours with few-second to sub-second resolution and clinically relevant precision. They are also adapted for minimally invasive subcutaneous placements (microneedles, indwelling needles) for interstitial fluid monitoring (e.g., brain, tumor, dermal ISF). The review highlights the importance of seconds-resolved time resolution and nanomolar limits of detection for hormones (achieved for LH and NGAL, micromolar for others). Time delays between subcutaneous ISF and plasma concentrations (e.g., 5-12 min for glucose, ~17 min for vancomycin) and correlations (strong for cortisol, <6% error for glucose) are noted, influenced by target properties. No dose-response comparisons for sensor parameters or monitoring duration were explicitly reported.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Increased secretion during stress; exhibits complex temporal patterns, including ultradian, circadian, and stress-induced oscillations, with high variability.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Levels in saliva and blood are strongly correlated. Typically rises ~3-5 min after HPA axis activation, peaking ~30 min later. Ultradian (every 60 min), circadian (decreases during day), and stress-induced (within minutes) oscillations are observed. Social and emotional experiences can account for over 70% of variation.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Primary end product of the HPA axis; mediates stress response, energy mobilization, increased arousal and vigilance, inhibition of nonessential anabolic activity, and regulation of various physiological functions.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Stress, HPA (hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal) axis activity, acute response to stress, social and emotional experiences, monitoring of cumulative stress and insufficient recovery.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of stress and HPA axis function; dysregulation associated with overtraining, functional over-reaching, and non-functional overreaching syndromes; contributes to adaptations during acute stress; relevant for monitoring cumulative stress and insufficient recovery and performance status.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Levels in subcutaneous ISF parallel plasma levels with a time delay.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Subcutaneous glucose levels parallel plasma glucose levels with a time delay of 5 to 12 min and an error of less than 6%.

analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of health and performance status; commercially available sensor for continuous monitoring.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Varies in pulse amplitude and frequency
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: High pulse frequencies (every 60 min or less) stimulate LH synthesis and secretion; low pulse frequencies (every 3 h) stimulate FSH synthesis and secretion.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Released from the hypothalamus to stimulate the release of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) from the anterior pituitary gland.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Governs the synthesis and secretion of LH and FSH; indicator of HPG axis function and integrity.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Stimulated by high GnRH pulse frequencies; pulsatility varies significantly
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Stimulated at high GnRH pulse frequencies (every 60 min or less). Pulsatility varies throughout the menstrual cycle: every 1 to 2 h during follicular phase, every 4 h during luteal phase, and peaks just before ovulation. In menopause or hypothalamic amenorrhea, pulsatility becomes rapid (~50 min) but can be disordered, suppressed, or non-existent. EAB sensors achieve nanomolar limits of detection.

analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Monitoring can help tailor training and inform exercise and recovery intervals; indicator of HPG axis function and integrity; dysregulation contributes to overtraining syndromes.
